sources: Gateway Arch National Park Superintendent's Compendium for 2026

trails.trailTip: This flat, paved path along the Mississippi is stroller- and wheelchair-friendly, but it can flood and close temporarily after heavy rain upstream — check current park alerts before visiting if the river has been running high.
trails.didYouKnow: The Riverfront Trail runs directly below the Arch's east leg, offering one of the few vantage points where you can see the monument's full 630-foot height reflected in the Mississippi.

trails.trailTip: A short, level downtown walk connecting the Arch grounds to Kiener Plaza — pleasant any time of day, though it crosses active city streets so use marked crosswalks.
trails.didYouKnow: Kiener Plaza is named for Olympic gymnast Walter Kiener and has served as a downtown gathering space since the 1960s, around the same time the Arch was completed.

trails.trailTip: A flat, paved loop around the Arch's base with some of the best close-up photo angles of the monument — arrive near sunrise or sunset for softer light and thinner crowds.
trails.didYouKnow: The Gateway Arch is the tallest man-made monument in the Western Hemisphere at 630 feet, and its footprint forms a perfect catenary curve.

trails.trailTip: A short landscaped walk linking the Old Courthouse to the Arch grounds — an easy add-on if you're visiting both sites in one trip.
trails.didYouKnow: The square is named for the St. Louis civic leader who championed creating the riverfront memorial in the 1930s, decades before the Arch itself was built.

trails.trailTip: A flat riverfront walk to the historic Eads Bridge; the bridge's pedestrian level offers a good elevated view back toward the Arch, though the approach ramps have some incline.
trails.didYouKnow: Opened in 1874, the Eads Bridge was the first bridge to cross the Mississippi River at St. Louis and one of the first large-scale uses of steel (rather than iron) in American bridge construction.

trails.trailTip: A quieter riverside stretch south of the main Arch grounds with far fewer visitors — good for an unhurried walk, though lighting and amenities are sparser after dark.
trails.didYouKnow: The area is named for Auguste Chouteau, a co-founder of St. Louis in 1764, whose original landing site was along this stretch of riverfront.

trails.trailTip: A long, flat paved promenade along the Mississippi popular with runners and cyclists as well as walkers — it can flood after major rain events upstream, so check current conditions if the river is high.
trails.didYouKnow: The riverwalk is named for Leonor K. Sullivan, a longtime U.S. Representative from St. Louis who championed federal support for the riverfront and the Arch grounds.

trails.trailTip: A brief loop around the 1839 Old Courthouse — pair it with a stop inside, which is free and staffed by NPS rangers with exhibits on the building's history.
trails.didYouKnow: The Old Courthouse was the site of the first two trials of Dred Scott v. Sandford in 1847 and 1850, a case that helped set the stage for the Civil War.

animals.whereToLook: High on the Arch itself, visible from the grounds below
animals.viewingTip: Watch from the grounds with binoculars rather than trying to get closer — the Arch's exterior isn't publicly accessible near the nest anyway, and that distance is exactly what lets the falcons nest undisturbed in the middle of a city.
animals.didYouKnow: The Arch is one of the tallest urban peregrine falcon nest sites in the country, part of a decades-long recovery for a species that was nearly wiped out east of the Rockies by DDT.

animals.whereToLook: Along the Mississippi riverfront and nearby ponds
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy watching mallards from the paths without feeding them — bread and other human food harm waterfowl digestion and draw unnaturally large, aggressive flocks to busy walkways.
animals.didYouKnow: Mallards are the ancestor of nearly all domestic duck breeds except the Muscovy duck.

animals.whereToLook: Lawns and trees throughout the Arch grounds
animals.viewingTip: Watch squirrels forage naturally rather than hand-feeding them; a fed squirrel loses its wariness of people and is more likely to bite or be hit crossing busy park roads.
animals.didYouKnow: Eastern gray squirrels bury far more nuts than they ever retrieve, making them one of the region's most effective (if accidental) tree planters.

animals.whereToLook: Along the Mississippi riverbank near the grounds
animals.viewingTip: Watch from the paved riverfront paths with binoculars rather than approaching the water's edge where a heron is fishing, which will simply flush the bird before you get a good look.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite their size, great blue herons weigh only 5-6 pounds thanks to hollow bones, an adaptation shared with all flying birds.

animals.whereToLook: Native plantings in the Explorers' Garden near the visitor center
animals.viewingTip: Observe and photograph monarchs on the milkweed and nectar plantings without handling them — resting migrants need every bit of stored energy for the journey south to Mexico.
animals.didYouKnow: Monarchs that pass through St. Louis in fall may be flying all the way to overwintering sites in the oyamel fir forests of central Mexico, a multi-generational round trip.

animals.whereToLook: Soaring above the Arch grounds and riverfront
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy watching hawks soar and hunt from a distance with binoculars — resist any urge to approach if one is seen perched low with prey, since that's exactly when it's most easily flushed.
animals.didYouKnow: Red-tailed hawks are highly adaptable to cities, often nesting on tall buildings or bridge structures that mimic the cliff ledges they'd use in the wild.

animals.viewingTip: Give nesting or goslings-with-parents groups plenty of room and never feed geese — fed, habituated geese become more aggressive toward visitors and their droppings concentrate on lawns people use.
animals.didYouKnow: Many Canada geese found in St. Louis parks today are non-migratory year-round residents rather than the long-distance migrants the species is famous for.

animals.whereToLook: Shallow water along the Mississippi riverbank
animals.viewingTip: Watch carp cruising the shallows from the bank or a bridge rather than wading in after them — the riverbank here can be steep, muddy, and swift-flowing.
animals.didYouKnow: Common carp are not native to North America; they were introduced from Europe and Asia in the 1800s and are now widespread throughout the Mississippi River system.
